# Week 13 - Statistical Modeling and Quarto

## Import data

## Part 1: Setting Up Quarto
### 1.3 First Chunk: Load the Data
```{python}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import patsy
from plotnine import *

ecv = pd.read_csv("~/Documents/UT/comp_paleo/part3_AL/week11/ecv_by_specimen.csv")

# Put the grades in evolutionary order (otherwise they sort alphabetically)
grade_order = ["archaic", "mega", "trans", "pre.mod"]
ecv["grade"] = pd.Categorical(ecv["grade"], categories=grade_order, ordered=True)

print(ecv.shape)
print("Missing grades:", ecv["grade"].isna().sum())
ecv.head()
```

## Part 2: Patsy Deisgn Matrics
### 2.1 Build Patsy Design Matrices
```{python}
#| label: design-matrix-simple

import patsy

y, X = patsy.dmatrices("ecv_median_cm3 ~ age_mid_Ma", data=ecv, return_type="dataframe")
print("Response (y):")
print(y.head())
print("\nDesign matrix (X):")
print(X.head())
print("\nX columns:", X.columns.tolist())
```

Question 2.1: What are the two columns in X? What is the value of the intercept column for every row, and why?

   - X is a matrix rather than a series. The two columns are vectors of 1s and X values. Intercept is fitting a linear model to estimate the slope and vertical offset.

### 2.2 Build a Multiple Deisgn Matrix
```{python}
#| label: design-matrix-multiple

y2, X2 = patsy.dmatrices(
    "ecv_median_cm3 ~ age_mid_Ma + C(grade)", data=ecv, return_type="dataframe"
)
print("X2 shape:", X2.shape)
print("X2 columns:", X2.columns.tolist())
print(X2.head(8))
```
Question 2.2: How many columns does X2 have, and what does each one represent? Which grade is the reference level (the one that does NOT get its own dummy column)?

 - X2 has 5 columns. Each column represents the Intercept, dummy variables: grade[T.meg], grade[T.trans], and grade[T.pre.mod] representing the different levels in my categorical variable, and the age_mid_Ma. Archaic is the reference level becasue we defined the caterogical order. 

 ### 2.3 Inspect the Encoding
```{python}
#| label: inspect-encoding

col = "C(grade)[T.mega]"
rows = X2.index[X2[col] == 1]
print(f"Rows where {col} == 1:")
print(ecv.loc[rows, ["taxon", "grade", "ecv_median_cm3", "age_mid_Ma"]].head())
```

## Fitting a Model
```{python}
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

# Fit: smf.ols takes the same formula string Patsy does
model = smf.ols("ecv_median_cm3 ~ age_mid_Ma", data=ecv).fit()

# Print the full results table
print(model.summary())
```

## Accessing Results Programmatically
```{python}
# Individual attributes
print("R-squared:", model.rsquared)
print("Intercept:", model.params["Intercept"])
print("Slope on age:", model.params["age_mid_Ma"])
print("p-value on age:", model.pvalues["age_mid_Ma"])

# Predicted values and residuals
ecv["fitted"] = model.fittedvalues
ecv["resid"] = model.resid
```

## Part 3: OLS Regression
### 3.1 Simple Regression: ECV ~age
```{python}
#| label: ols-simple

model1 = smf.ols("ecv_median_cm3 ~ age_mid_Ma", data=ecv).fit()
print(model1.summary())
```

Question 3.1 Report the slope, its p-value, and the R-squared. Is ECV significantly associated with age in this model? What does the sign of the slope tell you biologically?

 - Slope = -249.14, p-value < 0.0001, R-squared: 0.750 or 75% of the variance. Yes, ECV is significantly associated with age. Biologically, this reflects the overall trend of increased brain size in the hominin lineage, from small-brained early hominins to the larger brains of later Homo.

### 3.2 Multiple Regression: ECV ~age + grade
```{python}
#| label: ols-multiple

model2 = smf.ols("ecv_median_cm3 ~ age_mid_Ma + C(grade)", data=ecv).fit()
print(model2.summary())
```

Question 3.2: Compare R-squared between model1 and model2. Does adding grade improve fit? Interpret the C(grade)[T.pre.mod] coefficient what do its sign and size tell you about pre.mod specimens compared with archaic specimens of the same age?

 - Adding grade did improve the fit as the R-squared increased from 75% to 80%. As more parameters are introduced, the fit will improve. Adding grade also reduced the age slope from −294 to −226 cm3/Ma, meaning part of the age effect in model1 reflected which grades are present at different times. The coefficient of C(grade)[T.pre.mod] is 113.1 cm3. Because archaic is the reference grade and age is in the model, this is the difference in predicted ECV between a pre.mod specimen and an archaic specimen of the same age. The sign is positive and the size is about 113 cm3. 

 ### 3.3 Residual diagnostic plot
 ```{python}
 #| label: fig-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals vs. Fitted Values for the Multiple Regression Model"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4

ecv_diag = ecv.copy()
ecv_diag['fitted'] = model2.fittedvalues
ecv_diag['resid'] = model2.resid

(
    ggplot(ecv_diag, aes(x='fitted', y='resid'))
    + geom_point(alpha=0.5)
    + geom_hline(yintercept=0, color='red', linetype='dashed')
    + labs(x='Fitted values', y='Residuals',
           title='Residuals vs. Fitted')
    + theme_bw()
)
```

Question 3.3: Describe the pattern (or lack of pattern) in the residual plot. Are there any obvious outliers or trends that suggest the OLS assumptions are violated?
 - Residuals are not great. U-shaped

```{python}
#| label: ols-interaction

model3 = smf.ols("ecv_median_cm3 ~ age_mid_Ma * C(grade)", data=ecv).fit()
print(model3.summary())
```

## Part 4: Figures and Inline Results in Quarto
### 4.1 A polished figure with a cross-reference
```{python}
#| label: fig-ecv-fitted
#| fig-cap: "Observed ECV and OLS fitted line (ECV ~ age). Points colored by grade."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5

pred = pd.DataFrame(
    {"age_mid_Ma": np.linspace(ecv["age_mid_Ma"].min(), ecv["age_mid_Ma"].max(), 200)}
)
pred["ecv_pred"] = model1.predict(pred)

(
    ggplot(
        ecv, aes(x="age_mid_Ma", y="ecv_median_cm3", color="grade", size="n_estimates")
    )
    + geom_point(alpha=0.6, size=2)
    + geom_line(
        aes(x="age_mid_Ma", y="ecv_pred"),
        data=pred,
        color="black",
        size=1,
        inherit_aes=False,
    )
    + scale_x_reverse()
    + labs(x="Age (Ma)", y="ECV (cm³)", color="Grade", title="Hominin ECV Through Time")
    + theme_bw()
)
```

As shown in @fig-ecv-fitted, ECV increases toward the present, though considerable variation is present across grades.

 ### 4.2 Inline Python Results

The simple regression explains `{python} round(model1.rsquared, 3)` of the variance in ECV. For every additional million years into the past, ECV decreases by `{python} abs(round(model1.params['age_mid_Ma'], 1))` cc on average (p = `{python} round(model1.pvalues['age_mid_Ma'], 4)`).

### 4.3 A Model Comparison Table
```{python}
#| label: tbl-model-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of three OLS models for ECV"

comparison = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Model": ["ECV ~ age", "ECV ~ age + C(grade)", "ECV ~ age * C(grade)"],
        "R-squared": [round(m.rsquared, 3) for m in [model1, model2, model3]],
        "Adj. R-squared": [round(m.rsquared_adj, 3) for m in [model1, model2, model3]],
        "AIC": [round(m.aic, 1) for m in [model1, model2, model3]],
        "N": [int(m.nobs) for m in [model1, model2, model3]],
    }
)
comparison
```
